procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated March 28, 1968 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 380 of 1968, summarily dismissing the appellant's appeal against his conviction under Sections 326 and 324 I.P.C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant was convicted by the Additional Sessions Judge for offences under Sections 326 and 324 I.P.C. He appealed to the Bombay High Court, which dismissed the appeal with one word: "dismissed."
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution. The appellant contended that the injuries were inflicted in self-defense, and challenged the trial court's reliance on witness statements made in the committing court.

directions: The appellant will surrender to his bail bond to serve out the remaining sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in summarily dismissing a criminal appeal with a single word "dismissed" without providing any reasons, especially when arguable points were raised.

facts: The appellant was convicted by an Additional Sessions Judge for offences under Sections 326 and 324 of the Indian Penal Code.
He filed a criminal appeal in the High Court against his conviction.
The High Court summarily dismissed the appeal with a single word: "dismissed", without providing any reasons.
The Supreme Court, upon reviewing the case, found that the appeal raised arguable points.
law: Section 410 of the Criminal Procedure Code grants a person convicted by a Sessions Judge a right of appeal to the High Court. This right includes the ability to challenge conclusions of fact and request a reappraisal of evidence.
Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal. The judicious exercise of this power is aided by reasoned orders from lower courts.
application: The Supreme Court stated that it has repeatedly pointed out that when a criminal appeal raises arguable points, the High Court should provide some reasons for its decision, even if brief.
A non-reasoned, one-word dismissal is improper because it undermines the statutory right of appeal granted by Section 410 Cr.P.C., which entitles the appellant to a reappraisal of evidence.
The Court explained that without the benefit of the High Court's opinion, the Supreme Court feels "embarrassed" in dealing with the points raised on appeal under Article 136.
For the Supreme Court to properly exercise its discretionary power, it expects High Courts to issue "speaking orders" (orders with reasons), however sketchy, especially in cases with arguable points.
The Court warned that the absence of a speaking order might force it to remand cases back to the High Court for rehearing, causing avoidable delay and harassment to the accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was incorrect to summarily dismiss the criminal appeal with the single word "dismissed." It ruled that when an appeal raises arguable points, the High Court is obligated to provide reasons for its decision to enable the Supreme Court to properly exercise its appellate jurisdiction and to ensure the statutory right of appeal is meaningful.

issue.issue_text: Whether statements made by witnesses in the committing court, from which they later resiled during the trial, can be treated as substantive evidence under Section 288, Cr.P.C. and form the basis for a conviction.

facts: Three eyewitnesses supported the prosecution's case in the committing court but later changed their statements (resiled) during the trial.
These earlier statements from the committing court were formally brought onto the trial record under Section 288 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
law: The Supreme Court affirmed that statements made by witnesses in a committing court, when brought on record under Section 288, Cr.P.C., constitute substantive evidence.
This means such statements are not merely for contradicting the witness but can be used to prove the facts of the case.
application: The Court established a condition for using such evidence: the court must be satisfied that the earlier statements (from the committing court) were true, while the later statements made at trial were untrue.
In this specific case, the Court found that the witnesses' statements at trial were 'unconvincing' and that there was likely an 'ulterior motive' for them to change their story.
Conversely, the Court found that the earlier statements made in the committing court 'appeared to have a ring of truth about them'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the earlier statements were deemed true and the later ones false, they could be safely relied upon to sustain the appellant's conviction. Therefore, the trial court was correct in using these resiled statements as the basis for its judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the quantum of sentence in an appeal under Article 136, particularly when the High Court has erroneously dismissed the appeal summarily.

facts: The appellant appealed their conviction and sentence to the High Court.
The High Court dismissed the appeal summarily with a one-word order, "dismissed", without providing any reasons.
The case presented arguable points on both facts and law.
law: The Supreme Court normally does not interfere with the quantum of a sentence in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
High Courts are expected to provide reasons, however brief, when dismissing an appeal that raises arguable points, to allow the Supreme Court to properly exercise its discretionary power.
application: The Court found that the High Court's summary dismissal without reasons was erroneous.
This error created an exception to the general rule of non-interference with sentencing.
The Court decided that to avoid further delay that would be caused by remanding the case back to the High Court, it was a "fit case" to examine the question of the sentence itself.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided to interfere with the sentence because the High Court had erroneously dismissed the appeal summarily without giving reasons. The Court held that this failure by the High Court created an exceptional circumstance, making it a fit case for the Supreme Court to consider the sentence directly to avoid further delay.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal under Article 136, should reappraise the evidence itself when the High Court has summarily dismissed the appeal without giving reasons.

facts: An appellant, convicted by a Sessions Judge, appealed to the High Court.
The High Court dismissed the appeal summarily with the single word "dismissed", providing no reasons for its decision.
The appellant then appealed to the Supreme Court under Article 136, raising what the Supreme Court considered to be "arguable points" on both facts and law.
law: The Supreme Court is normally reluctant to reappraise evidence in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, as this is the primary function of the High Court.

The Court has repeatedly stated that when an appeal raises arguable points, the High Court should provide reasons for its decision, even if brief, to enable the Supreme Court to properly exercise its discretionary power.
When a High Court fails to provide a reasoned order, the Supreme Court may have to remand the case back to the High Court for re-hearing and a reasoned decision.
application: The Court first held that the High Court's summary dismissal without reasons was "not right" because the appeal clearly raised arguable points.

The Court then considered its options. It acknowledged that one option was to remand the case back to the High Court, but this would cause "avoidable harassment of the accused persons and delay in the final disposal" of the case.
To avoid this further delay, the Court decided to make an exception to its normal practice.
It chose to "go into the evidence ourselves" and conduct the reappraisal that the High Court should have done.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided to accept the responsibility of reappraising the evidence itself. Although this is a course it is normally reluctant to adopt, it did so in this instance to avoid the further delay and harassment to the appellant that would have been caused by remanding the case back to the High Court, which had erred by summarily dismissing the appeal without giving any reasons.

If the court is satisfied that the earlier statements were true and the later statements at trial were untrue, the earlier statements can be safely relied upon to sustain a conviction.
In this case, the earlier statements had a 'ring of truth' while the statements at trial were unconvincing, suggesting an ulterior motive for the witnesses to resile.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a criminal appeal filed in the High Court under Section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure raises arguable points of fact or law, the High Court cannot summarily dismiss it without providing reasons, as the statutory right of appeal entitles the convicted person to a reappraisal of evidence.
obiter: Statements made by witnesses in a committing court, which are brought on record at trial under Section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, constitute substantive evidence and can be relied upon to sustain a conviction if the court is satisfied that those earlier statements were true and the later trial testimony was not.

While the Supreme Court does not normally interfere with the quantum of a sentence on an appeal under Article 136, it may do so if the High Court has erroneously dismissed the appeal without giving reasons.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that while the conviction was correctly based on the substantive evidence of prior statements made by witnesses who later resiled, the High Court committed a serious error by summarily dismissing the criminal appeal with a single word. This failure of the High Court to provide reasons on arguable points forced the Supreme Court to undertake a full reappraisal of the evidence itself, which it normally avoids. Upon review, the Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence due to mitigating circumstances surrounding the incident.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 288, Cr.P.C., statements made by witnesses in the committing court constitute substantive evidence, and if a court is satisfied that those earlier statements were true and the later statements at trial were untrue, the earlier statements can be safely relied upon to sustain a conviction.
why_appellant_lost: The court determined that the statements made by the eyewitnesses in the committing court, which were brought on record under Section 288 Cr.P.C., constituted substantive evidence that could form the basis of a conviction.
The court found the witnesses' earlier statements to have a 'ring of truth about them,' while their later statements at trial were 'unconvincing,' suggesting an ulterior motive for resiling.
After reviewing the evidence, the court was 'unable to hold that the injuries in question had been inflicted on the prosecution witnesses by the appellant while acting in self;defence.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that statements under Section 288 Cr.P.C. are substantive evidence was affirmed, with the court stating that if it is satisfied the earlier statements were true and the later ones false, 'then the earlier statements can safely be relied upon to sustain the conviction.'
The court's own appraisal of the evidence led it to conclude that the trial court was correct in its assessment of the witnesses' credibility and in convicting the appellant.
policy_considerations: An appeal under Section 410 Cr.P.C. confers a statutory right on a convicted person to challenge conclusions of fact and claim a reappraisal of evidence, which is nullified by a summary dismissal without reasons.

High Courts should provide reasoned orders, however sketchy, when dismissing appeals that raise arguable points, as this enables the Supreme Court to satisfactorily exercise its discretionary power under Article 136.

The absence of a reasoned order from the High Court may force the Supreme Court to either remand the case, causing 'avoidable harassment of the accused persons concerned and delay,' or to undertake a full evidence review itself, a course it is normally reluctant to adopt.
